Chapter 6: Crossing Boundaries—Encounters with the “Other”
You know, sometimes the biggest changes in our lives start with just a single conversation.
For the doctor, life outside Gaza always felt far away—almost like something from a distant story, shaped more by headlines than by real people.
But when his work brought him face-to-face with folks from across the divide, those old lines between “us” and “them” started to fade.
There was one day that sticks out—he was called in to treat a little boy from a neighboring community. Now, to a lot of people, that community was seen as the enemy.
The boy’s parents showed up at the hospital, their faces drawn tight with worry and that kind of uncertainty you just can’t hide. The doctor could see how they hesitated, not sure if they could trust him.
But as he checked over their son, politics didn’t matter. All that mattered was the child’s pain, and how to help him.
In the quiet of the treatment room, something changed. The parents watched the doctor’s steady hands, saw the gentle way he spoke to their son. There was real care in his eyes.
When the procedure was finished, relief just washed over the family. The mother, her voice trembling, thanked him—not just for his medical skill, but for seeing her child as a person, not an enemy.
And you know, moments like this started to happen more often. The doctor found himself at conferences and meetings where people from both sides would gather. There was always a bit of suspicion—a guarded hope hanging in the air.
He’d listen to stories of loss, stories full of fear. And in each one, he recognized pieces of his own experience.
Sometimes, those conversations got heated. Voices rose, frustration and pain spilling out. But underneath it all, there was this quiet longing—people just wanted to be understood. They wanted to be seen, and heard.
It became so clear: no matter which side you’re born on, most people want the same things. Safety. Dignity. A future their kids can believe in.
The doctor realized that the walls built by conflict aren’t just made of concrete or barbed wire. They’re built out of fear, misunderstandings, and old wounds.
Sure, those walls don’t come down overnight. But every honest conversation, every act of kindness and empathy? It chips away at those foundations.
He began to see himself as more than just a healer of bodies—he was becoming a bridge between worlds.
By sharing his own story, and by truly listening to others, he helped create little spaces where trust could start to grow.
It wasn’t easy. Sometimes, it was slow, even frustrating. But it offered a glimpse of what’s possible—if enough people are willing to reach across that divide.
